items.stem: What is the name for "a fat or oil, made from fatty acids and glycerol and containing C, H and O"?
items.answer: Lipid
items.markingKey: Lipid: a fat or oil, made from fatty acids and glycerol and containing C, H and O.

items.stem: Explain why plants store glucose as starch rather than as glucose.
items.answer: Starch is insoluble, so it does not affect the water potential of cells (no osmosis) and it is compact; glucose is soluble and would draw water in.
items.markingKey: insoluble [1]; does not affect osmosis / water potential [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why proteins can have many different shapes and functions.
items.answer: They are made from about 20 different amino acids joined in different sequences; the sequence determines how the chain folds, giving each protein a specific shape.
items.markingKey: different amino acids / sequence [1]; sequence determines shape [1] [2]

items.stem: Which smaller molecules join together to form proteins?
items.answer: amino acids
items.markingKey: Proteins is made from amino acids.

items.stem: Name the smaller units used to make each molecule: (i) fats and oils, (ii) proteins, (iii) glycogen.
items.answer: (i) fatty acids and glycerol (ii) amino acids (iii) glucose
items.markingKey: (i) fatty acids and glycerol; (ii) amino acids; (iii) glucose (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: Arjun is studying the molecules in a potato. The main molecules present are starch and cellulose. (a) State the chemical elements present in cellulose. (b) Describe one function of starch in living organisms. (c) Suggest how a scientist could show that this food contains protein.
items.answer: (a) C, H, O. (b) Energy store in plants. (c) Add biuret reagent; a purple colour shows protein is present.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) biuret [1]; purple [1] [2]

items.stem: Which element is found in proteins but not in carbohydrates or fats?
items.answer: Nitrogen
items.markingKey: Proteins contain C, H, O and N (and sometimes S); carbohydrates and fats contain only C, H and O.

items.stem: Explain why animals and plants need nitrogen-containing compounds in their diet or from the soil.
items.answer: Nitrogen is needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins for growth, enzymes and repair (and DNA).
items.markingKey: amino acids / proteins contain N [1]; needed for growth/enzymes [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare the structure of glycogen and cellulose.
items.answer: Both are large carbohydrates made of many glucose units containing C, H and O. Glycogen is an energy store in animals; cellulose forms plant cell walls and the glucose units are joined differently.
items.markingKey: one similarity [1]; one difference [1] [2]

items.stem: A molecule contains C, H, O and is used for this function: energy store in animals (liver and muscles). Which molecule is it?
items.answer: glycogen
items.markingKey: Glycogen: carbohydrate made of glucose; energy store in animals (liver and muscles).

items.stem: Name the smaller units used to make each molecule: (i) starch, (ii) cellulose, (iii) glycogen.
items.answer: (i) glucose (ii) glucose (iii) glucose
items.markingKey: (i) glucose; (ii) glucose; (iii) glucose (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: Complete the information for each molecule by naming the smaller units it is made from and the elements it contains: (i) cellulose, (ii) fats and oils, (iii) glycogen.
items.answer: (i) glucose; C, H, O (ii) fatty acids and glycerol; C, H, O (iii) glucose; C, H, O
items.markingKey: (i) glucose [1], C, H, O [1]; (ii) fatty acids and glycerol [1], C, H, O [1]; (iii) glucose [1], C, H, O [1] [6]

items.stem: Hana is studying the molecules in a peanut. The main molecules present are fats and oils and proteins. (a) Name the smaller molecules from which fats and oils are made. (b) State the chemical elements present in proteins. (c) Explain why large molecules must be broken down into smaller molecules during digestion. (d) Suggest how a scientist could show that this food contains protein.
items.answer: (a) fatty acids and glycerol. (b) C, H, O, N (and sometimes S). (c) Large molecules are insoluble / too big to pass through the gut wall into the blood; small soluble molecules can be absorbed. (d) Add biuret reagent; a purple colour shows protein is present.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) too large / insoluble [1]; small molecules absorbed [1] [2] (d) biuret [1]; purple [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "iodine test"?
options: A test for fats and oils: shaking with ethanol then adding water gives a cloudy white emulsion.
A test for reducing sugars: heated blue solution gives a brick-red precipitate.
A test for starch: orange-brown iodine solution turns blue-black.
A test for protein: blue biuret solution turns purple.
items.answer: A test for starch: orange-brown iodine solution turns blue-black.
items.markingKey: Iodine test: a test for starch: orange-brown iodine solution turns blue-black.

items.stem: Explain why the colour of Benedict's test can be used to estimate the amount of reducing sugar.
items.answer: More reducing sugar gives more precipitate, so the colour changes further from blue through green, yellow and orange to brick-red.
items.markingKey: colour sequence [1]; more sugar → further along / more precipitate [1] [2]

items.stem: Sucrose solution gives a negative result with Benedict's solution. Explain why it gives a positive result after boiling with dilute acid and neutralising.
items.answer: Sucrose is not a reducing sugar; acid hydrolyses (breaks) it into glucose and fructose, which are reducing sugars.
items.markingKey: sucrose non-reducing [1]; broken into reducing sugars [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena tested food samples. Results: sample P: DCPIP → blue, biuret → blue, Benedict's (heated) → blue; sample Q: DCPIP → blue, biuret → purple, Benedict's (heated) → blue. State which nutrients each sample contains.
items.answer: P: none of those tested; Q: protein
items.markingKey: P: none of those tested; Q: protein (1 mark per sample fully correct) [2]

items.stem: Arjun tested food samples. Results: sample P: ethanol emulsion → clear, iodine → blue-black, Benedict's (heated) → blue, DCPIP → blue; sample Q: ethanol emulsion → clear, iodine → orange-brown, Benedict's (heated) → blue, DCPIP → blue; sample R: ethanol emulsion → clear, iodine → orange-brown, Benedict's (heated) → brick-red precipitate, DCPIP → colourless. State which nutrients each sample contains.
items.answer: P: starch; Q: none of those tested; R: reducing sugar, vitamin C
items.markingKey: P: starch; Q: none of those tested; R: reducing sugar, vitamin C (1 mark per sample fully correct) [3]

items.stem: Mateo tested food samples. Results: sample P: biuret → blue, Benedict's (heated) → brick-red precipitate, iodine → orange-brown, DCPIP → blue; sample Q: biuret → blue, Benedict's (heated) → blue, iodine → orange-brown, DCPIP → blue; sample R: biuret → blue, Benedict's (heated) → blue, iodine → blue-black, DCPIP → blue. State which nutrients each sample contains. Suggest the identity of one sample from this list: cheese, egg white, potato, rice flour.
items.answer: P: reducing sugar; Q: none of those tested; R: starch. A sample with these results could be potato.
items.markingKey: P: reducing sugar; Q: none of those tested; R: starch (1 mark per sample fully correct); identity consistent with results [1] [4]

items.stem: Felix wants to find out whether onion contains reducing sugar, and to compare the amount with another food. (a) Describe how to test the food for reducing sugar. (b) State the result you would expect if the nutrient is absent.
items.answer: (a) Prepare a solution/suspension of the food; Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath; positive result: brick-red (or green/yellow/orange) precipitate. (b) Stays blue.
items.markingKey: (a) preparing sample (crush with water) [1]; reagent / method: Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath [1]; positive result brick-red (or green/yellow/orange) precipitate [1] [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Kwame wants to find out whether banana contains starch, and to compare the amount with another food. (a) State the result you would expect if the nutrient is absent. (b) Describe a suitable control for this test. (c) Suggest how the method could be changed to compare the amount of the nutrient in two foods. (d) State one safety precaution for this test.
items.answer: (a) Stays orange-brown. (b) Repeat the test using distilled water instead of the food sample. (c) Use the same mass of each food in the same volume of water and the same volume of reagent; compare colour intensity (or use a colour chart / colorimeter, or count drops for DCPIP). (d) Wear eye protection.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) same mass / volume [1]; compare colour or quantitative method [1] [2] (d) [1]

items.stem: Which food test requires heating?
items.answer: Benedict's test for reducing sugars
items.markingKey: Benedict's solution must be heated in a water bath (about 80 °C) for the colour change.

items.stem: Explain why a control tube containing water instead of food should be set up for each food test.
items.answer: It shows the colour of the reagent with no nutrient present, so a colour change in the food tube can be identified as a positive result.
items.markingKey: comparison [1]; shows change is due to the food [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the emulsion test must not be done near a flame.
items.answer: Ethanol is highly flammable.

items.stem: Explain how the DCPIP test can compare the vitamin C content of two fruit juices.
items.answer: Add each juice drop by drop to a fixed volume of DCPIP until it just becomes colourless; the fewer drops (smaller volume) needed, the more vitamin C the juice contains.
items.markingKey: fixed volume of DCPIP [1]; count drops to decolourise [1]; fewer drops = more vitamin C [1] [3]

items.stem: A food sample gives these results: ethanol emulsion → cloudy white, DCPIP → blue, biuret → purple. Which nutrient does it contain?
items.answer: protein
items.markingKey: biuret → purple shows protein.

items.stem: Ines found that 1.5 cm³ of a 0.5 mg/cm³ vitamin C solution was needed to decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP. To decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP, 3.75 cm³ of orange juice and 6 cm³ of apple juice were needed. (a) Calculate the concentration of vitamin C in each juice. (b) State which juice contains more vitamin C.
items.answer: (a) orange juice: 0.200 mg/cm³; apple juice: 0.125 mg/cm³ (b) orange juice
items.markingKey: (a) mass of vitamin C to decolourise = 0.75 mg [1]; 0.75 ÷ 3.75 = 0.200 [1]; ÷ 6 = 0.125 mg/cm³ [1] (b) orange juice (smaller volume needed) [1] [4]

items.stem: Omar tested food samples. Results: sample P: Benedict's (heated) → blue, biuret → blue, ethanol emulsion → cloudy white; sample Q: Benedict's (heated) → blue, biuret → blue, ethanol emulsion → clear. State which nutrients each sample contains.
items.answer: P: fat; Q: none of those tested
items.markingKey: P: fat; Q: none of those tested (1 mark per sample fully correct) [2]

items.stem: Describe how you would test a sample of food for starch, reducing sugar, protein and fat. Give the positive result for each test.
items.answer: Starch: iodine, orange-brown → blue-black. Reducing sugar: Benedict's, heat, blue → brick-red. Protein: biuret, blue → purple. Fat: ethanol then water, cloudy white emulsion.
items.markingKey: one mark per test with correct method and result [4]; control / safety point [1] [5]

(b) Suggest how the method could be changed to compare the amount of the nutrient in two foods. (c) State one safety precaution for this test.
items.answer: (a) Stays blue. (b) Use the same mass of each food in the same volume of water and the same volume of reagent; compare colour intensity (or use a colour chart / colorimeter, or count drops for DCPIP). (c) Wear eye protection; use a water bath, not a direct flame.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) same mass / volume [1]; compare colour or quantitative method [1] [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Felix wants to find out whether lemon juice contains vitamin C, and to compare the amount with another food. (a) Describe how to test the food for vitamin C. (b) State the result you would expect if the nutrient is absent. (c) Describe a suitable control for this test.
items.answer: (a) Prepare a solution/suspension of the food; DCPIP solution; positive result: blue DCPIP becomes colourless. (b) DCPIP stays blue. (c) Repeat the test using distilled water instead of the food sample.

items.markingKey: (a) preparing sample (crush with water) [1]; reagent / method: Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath [1]; positive result brick-red (or green/yellow/orange) precipitate [1] [3] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "gene"?
options: A length of DNA that codes for a protein.
The shape of a DNA molecule: two strands coiled around each other.
A long thread of DNA made up of many genes.
The pairing of bases between DNA strands: A always with T and C always with G.
items.answer: A length of DNA that codes for a protein.
items.markingKey: Gene: a length of DNA that codes for a protein.

items.stem: Explain why the amount of adenine in a DNA molecule is always equal to the amount of thymine.
items.answer: Every adenine on one strand pairs with a thymine on the other (complementary pairing), so they occur in equal numbers.
items.markingKey: A pairs only with T [1]; so numbers equal [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the structure of DNA allows it to carry genetic information.
items.answer: The sequence of bases along one strand forms a code; the order of bases in a gene determines the order of amino acids in a protein.
items.markingKey: base sequence = code [1]; determines amino acid order / protein [1] [2]

items.stem: One strand of a DNA molecule has the sequence G-A-T-G-T-C-T-A. Write the sequence of bases on the complementary strand.
items.answer: C-T-A-C-A-G-A-T
items.markingKey: C-T-A-C-A-G-A-T (all correct; deduct 1 mark per error) [2]

items.stem: One strand of a DNA molecule has the sequence C-G-G-T-T-A-A-C-G-T-A-C. Write the sequence of bases on the complementary strand. Then state how many adenine bases there are in this 12-base-pair section of DNA.
items.answer: G-C-C-A-A-T-T-G-C-A-T-G; 6 adenine bases
items.markingKey: G-C-C-A-A-T-T-G-C-A-T-G (all correct [2], deduct 1 per error); adenine = A on first strand (3) + T on first strand (3) = 6 [1] [3]

items.stem: A student builds a model of a short section of DNA. One strand has the base sequence TACTATGCG. (a) Write the sequence of the complementary strand. (b) Describe the overall shape of the DNA molecule.
items.answer: (a) ATGATACGC (b) Two strands coiled into a double helix, with bases paired in the middle.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) two strands [1]; double helix [1] [2]

items.stem: Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
items.answer: Thymine
items.markingKey: A–T and C–G.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term chromosome.
items.answer: A long thread of DNA made up of many genes.
items.markingKey: A long thread of DNA made up of many genes. Main idea [1] + precise detail [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why complementary base pairing allows DNA to be copied accurately.
items.answer: Each strand acts as a template: only A can pair with T and C with G, so the new strand has a sequence fixed by the old one.
items.markingKey: template [1]; specific pairing gives identical copy [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei writes in a revision note: "DNA is a single strand of bases." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: DNA is two strands twisted into a double helix, joined by base pairs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: DNA is two strands twisted into a double helix, joined by base pairs. [2]

items.stem: In a sample of DNA, 30% of the bases are adenine (A). Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases.
items.answer: thymine 30%; cytosine 20%; guanine 20%
items.markingKey: T = 30% (pairs with A) [1]; remaining 40% shared equally [1]; C = G = 20% [1] [3]

items.stem: In a sample of DNA, 24% of the bases are thymine (T). Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases.
items.answer: adenine 24%; cytosine 26%; guanine 26%
items.markingKey: A = 24% (pairs with T) [1]; remaining 52% shared equally [1]; C = G = 26% [1] [3]

items.stem: In a sample of DNA, 32% of the bases are adenine (A). Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases. If the section contains 12,000 bases in total, calculate the number of cytosine bases.
items.answer: thymine 32%; cytosine 18%; guanine 18%; 2,160 cytosine bases
items.markingKey: T = 32% (pairs with A) [1]; remaining 36% shared equally [1]; C = G = 18% [1]; 18% of 12,000 = 2,160 [1] [4]

items.stem: Which smaller molecules join to make starch?
items.answer: Glucose
items.markingKey: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of glucose units.

items.answer: Starch is made of many glucose molecules joined together.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Starch is made of many glucose molecules joined together. [2]

items.stem: Describe the chemical elements and smaller units that make up carbohydrates, fats and proteins, and give one function of each in the body.
items.answer: Carbohydrates: C, H, O; made of glucose / simple sugars; energy. Fats: C, H, O; fatty acids and glycerol; energy store / insulation. Proteins: C, H, O, N (S); amino acids; growth, repair, enzymes.

items.stem: A student in Doha states: "Benedict's test works at room temperature." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Benedict's test needs heating in a water bath.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Benedict's test needs heating in a water bath. [2]

items.stem: Sofia says: "Benedict's solution turns purple when protein is present." Explain whether Sofia is correct.
items.answer: Biuret solution turns purple with protein; Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugars.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Biuret solution turns purple with protein; Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugars. [2]

items.stem: Sipho found that 0.5 cm³ of a 2 mg/cm³ vitamin C solution was needed to decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP. To decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP, 2 cm³ of orange juice and 1.25 cm³ of mango juice were needed. (a) Calculate the concentration of vitamin C in each juice. (b) State which juice contains more vitamin C.
items.answer: (a) orange juice: 0.500 mg/cm³; mango juice: 0.800 mg/cm³ (b) mango juice
items.markingKey: (a) mass of vitamin C to decolourise = 1 mg [1]; 1 ÷ 2 = 0.500 [1]; ÷ 1.25 = 0.800 mg/cm³ [1] (b) mango juice (smaller volume needed) [1] [4]

items.stem: Nadia tested food samples. Results: sample P: iodine → blue-black, Benedict's (heated) → blue, DCPIP → blue; sample Q: iodine → orange-brown, Benedict's (heated) → blue, DCPIP → blue. State which nutrients each sample contains.
items.answer: P: starch; Q: none of those tested
items.markingKey: P: starch; Q: none of those tested (1 mark per sample fully correct) [2]

items.stem: Sofia found that 1.2 cm³ of a 1 mg/cm³ vitamin C solution was needed to decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP. To decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP, 0.6 cm³ of kiwi fruit juice and 0.9 cm³ of lemon juice were needed. (a) Calculate the concentration of vitamin C in each juice. (b) State which juice contains more vitamin C.
items.answer: (a) kiwi fruit juice: 2.00 mg/cm³; lemon juice: 1.33 mg/cm³ (b) kiwi fruit juice
items.markingKey: (a) mass of vitamin C to decolourise = 1.2 mg [1]; 1.2 ÷ 0.6 = 2.00 [1]; ÷ 0.9 = 1.33 mg/cm³ [1] (b) kiwi fruit juice (smaller volume needed) [1] [4]

items.stem: Omar wants to find out whether onion contains reducing sugar, and to compare the amount with another food. (a) Describe how to test the food for reducing sugar. (b) State one safety precaution for this test.
items.answer: (a) Prepare a solution/suspension of the food; Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath; positive result: brick-red (or green/yellow/orange) precipitate. (b) Wear eye protection; use a water bath, not a direct flame.
items.markingKey: (a) preparing sample (crush with water) [1]; reagent / method: Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath [1]; positive result brick-red (or green/yellow/orange) precipitate [1] [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Mei wants to find out whether egg white contains protein, and to compare the amount with another food. (a) Describe how to test the food for protein. (b) Describe a suitable control for this test. (c) State one safety precaution for this test.
items.answer: (a) Prepare a solution/suspension of the food; biuret solution; positive result: purple / violet. (b) Repeat the test using distilled water instead of the food sample. (c) Wear eye protection.
items.markingKey: (a) preparing sample (crush with water) [1]; reagent / method: biuret solution [1]; positive result purple / violet [1] [3] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: State the base pairing rules in DNA.
items.answer: A pairs with T; C pairs with G.
items.markingKey: both pairs [1]

items.stem: A student in Karachi states: "DNA is a single strand of bases." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: DNA is two strands twisted into a double helix, joined by base pairs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: DNA is two strands twisted into a double helix, joined by base pairs. [2]

items.stem: Diego says: "In DNA, adenine pairs with guanine." Explain whether Diego is correct.
items.answer: Adenine pairs with thymine; cytosine pairs with guanine.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Adenine pairs with thymine; cytosine pairs with guanine. [2]

items.stem: One strand of a DNA molecule has the sequence A-G-T-G-G-T-T-T. Write the sequence of bases on the complementary strand.
items.answer: T-C-A-C-C-A-A-A
items.markingKey: T-C-A-C-C-A-A-A (all correct; deduct 1 mark per error) [2]

items.stem: In a sample of DNA, 26% of the bases are adenine (A). Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases.
items.answer: thymine 26%; cytosine 24%; guanine 24%
items.markingKey: T = 26% (pairs with A) [1]; remaining 48% shared equally [1]; C = G = 24% [1] [3]

items.stem: A student builds a model of a short section of DNA. One strand has the base sequence CCTAAGACA. (a) Describe the overall shape of the DNA molecule. (b) Explain how a change in one base in this sequence could affect the protein produced. (c) Calculate the percentage of bases in this double-stranded section that are guanine or cytosine.
items.answer: (a) Two strands coiled into a double helix, with bases paired in the middle. (b) A change in base sequence (mutation) may change the amino acid coded for, changing the sequence and shape of the protein so it may not work. (c) 44.4%
items.markingKey: (a) two strands [1]; double helix [1] [2] (b) changes code / amino acid [1]; protein shape / function changed [1] [2] (c) G + C pairs = 4 of 9 pairs [1]; = 44.4% [1] [2]
